- TipTap licensing for commercial-adjacent use (open-source core vs paid collaboration features)
- BTCPay Server operational overhead for a demo project (may prefer NOWPayments for simplicity)
- Key rotation strategy when removing team members (the hardest crypto problem in M3 -- needs dedicated design)

## RESEARCH COMPLETE

**Project:** CipherBox Milestone 3
**Mode:** Ecosystem (Pitfalls dimension)
**Confidence:** MEDIUM-HIGH

### Key Findings

- **Editor library plaintext leakage is the highest-risk pitfall.** All mainstream collaboration libraries (Yjs y-websocket, Liveblocks, TipTap Cloud, Hocuspocus) relay plaintext operations through a central server by default. CipherBox must build a custom encrypted Yjs provider that encrypts all CRDT operations client-side before transmission. CryptPad and Proton Docs both spent significant effort solving this exact problem.

- **Team key distribution fundamentally changes the key hierarchy.** CipherBox currently wraps all keys with a single user's publicKey. Teams require a Per-Team Key (PTK) ECIES-wrapped for each member, with mandatory key rotation on member removal. Keybase's team crypto architecture is the closest reference implementation.

- **Autosave conflicts with IPNS publish latency.** IPNS publish takes 1-12 seconds. Document editors need saves every few seconds. These must be separated: CRDT sync happens in real-time via encrypted WebSocket, while IPNS persistence is debounced to 10-30 second intervals with a mutual-exclusion save queue.

- **Admin recovery without breaking ZK requires careful design.** The temptation to store a server-side recovery key must be resisted. Tresorit's model (ECIES-wrapped recovery key for designated admin) is the proven approach.

- **E-signature legal validity is not automatic.** A secp256k1 ECDSA signature is cryptographically valid but lacks the identity verification (CA), timestamping (TSA), and audit trail required for legal enforceability. For a tech demo, "cryptographic attestation" may suffice.

### Files Created

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.planning/research/m3/PITFALLS.md` | Domain pitfalls for M3 features (15 pitfalls across 4 feature areas) |

### Confidence Assessment

| Area | Level | Reason |
|------|-------|--------|
| Editor integration pitfalls | HIGH | CryptPad, Proton Docs, and ChainSafe research document these challenges extensively |
| Team key management pitfalls | HIGH | Keybase, Tresorit, and Bitwarden provide well-documented reference implementations |

1→# Feature Landscape: Milestone 3
     2→
     3→**Domain:** Encrypted productivity platform (docs, sheets, slides, teams, billing, signing)
     4→**Researched:** 2026-02-11
     5→**Confidence:** MEDIUM (grounded in competitor analysis; complexity estimates are informed approximations)
     6→
     7→## Context
     8→
     9→CipherBox already provides (M1) or will provide (M2) zero-knowledge encrypted file storage with IPFS/IPNS, Web3Auth, file/folder sharing, versioning, encrypted search, and vault export. Milestone 3 extends CipherBox from an encrypted file locker into a full encrypted productivity platform.
    10→
    11→The four feature pillars researched:
    12→
    13→1. Encrypted document editors (docs, sheets, slides)
    14→2. Team accounts (organizations, roles, permissions)
    15→3. Billing (Stripe + crypto/anonymous payments)
    16→4. Secure document signing (e-signatures)
    17→
    18→---
    19→
    20→## Feature 1: Encrypted Document Editing
    21→
    22→### How It Works in Zero-Knowledge Systems
    23→
    24→The dominant pattern, used by CryptPad, Skiff (discontinued), and Proton Docs, is:
    25→
    26→1. **CRDT-based collaboration** -- Conflict-free Replicated Data Types allow multiple clients to make concurrent edits that converge without a central authority resolving conflicts. Since the server never needs to understand document content, all CRDT updates can be end-to-end encrypted before transmission.
    27→
    28→2. **Symmetric document key** -- Each document has a random AES-256 key. All collaborators hold this key (distributed via ECIES key-wrapping, same pattern CipherBox already uses for folder keys). CRDT patches are encrypted with this key before being relayed through the server.
    29→
    30→3. **Relay server** -- The server acts as a dumb broadcast relay. It receives encrypted patches, stores them, and forwards them to other connected clients via WebSocket. It never decrypts.
    31→
    32→4. **Snapshots + patch log** -- To avoid replaying the entire document history on load, periodic encrypted snapshots are stored. CryptPad creates a checkpoint every 50 patches. New clients load the latest snapshot and apply subsequent patches.
    33→
    34→### Ecosystem of Editor Technologies
    35→
    36→| Technology | Type | Maturity | Encryption Support | Notes |
    37→|---|---|---|---|---|
    38→| Yjs | CRDT library | HIGH -- production at scale | Native -- designed for E2EE relay | Used by Skiff, Proton Docs (likely), many others |
    39→| Automerge | CRDT library | HIGH | Compatible -- needs wrapper | More academic, Rust core |
    40→| ChainPad | CRDT (blockchain-style) | MEDIUM | Native -- built for CryptPad | CryptPad-specific, not general purpose |
    41→| SecSync | E2EE CRDT relay protocol | MEDIUM | Purpose-built for E2EE | Built on top of Yjs, handles snapshot/update encryption |
    42→| TipTap | Rich text editor (ProseMirror) | HIGH | Via y-prosemirror binding | Best-in-class rich text editing DX |
    43→| ProseMirror | Low-level editor framework | HIGH | Via y-prosemirror | More control, more work |
    44→| CodeMirror | Code/text editor | HIGH | Via y-codemirror | Better for code/markdown |
    45→
    46→**Recommendation:** Use **Yjs + SecSync + TipTap** for documents. Yjs is the industry standard CRDT for collaborative editing. SecSync provides the encrypted relay protocol (snapshots, updates, ephemeral messages) purpose-built for E2EE over Yjs. TipTap provides a rich ProseMirror-based editor with excellent Yjs integration via y-prosemirror.
    47→
    48→### Document Types and Their Complexity
    49→
    50→| Document Type | Complexity | Why | Recommendation |
    51→|---|---|---|---|
    52→| Rich text (docs) | HIGH | Full formatting, images, tables, comments, suggestions | Build first -- TipTap/ProseMirror + Yjs is well-trodden |
    53→| Markdown notes | MEDIUM | Simpler model, no complex formatting state | Consider as simplified docs mode |
    54→| Spreadsheets | VERY HIGH | Cell dependencies, formulas, cross-references, charting | Defer or use minimal grid -- Proton Sheets took years |
    55→| Slides/presentations | HIGH | Layout engine, transitions, media, speaker notes | Defer -- CryptPad does markdown-only slides for a reason |
    56→| Whiteboard/drawing | MEDIUM-HIGH | Canvas state, shape manipulation, infinite canvas | Nice-to-have, not table stakes |
    57→
    58→**Key insight:** CryptPad, the most complete encrypted office suite, supports all these types but took a large team many years. Proton launched Docs in mid-2024 and Sheets in late 2025 -- over 18 months apart. Building even a basic encrypted rich text editor is a multi-month effort. Spreadsheets are an order of magnitude harder.

    72→| Export to common formats | PDF, Markdown, plain text export | MEDIUM | Client-side rendering + conversion |

    74→### Differentiators (Encrypted Docs)

    76→| Feature | Value Proposition | Complexity | Depends On |
    77→|---|---|---|---|
    78→| IPFS-backed document storage | Documents stored on decentralized infrastructure, not corporate servers | MEDIUM | Existing IPFS infrastructure |
    79→| Verifiable document integrity | IPFS CID proves document content has not been tampered with | LOW | Native IPFS property |
    80→| Client-side PDF export | Generate PDF entirely in browser, never touches server | MEDIUM | Browser PDF libraries (jsPDF, pdfmake) |

    96→---
    97→
    98→## Feature 2: Team Accounts
    99→
   100→### How It Works in Zero-Knowledge Systems
   101→
   102→The pattern, used by Tresorit, Cryptomator Hub, and Keeper, involves a key hierarchy:
   103→
   104→1. **Organization keypair** -- The org has a public/private key pair. The org private key is encrypted with the admin's personal key.
   105→
   106→2. **Team keypairs** -- Each team within the org has its own keypair. The team private key is encrypted with the org key (and optionally with each team member's personal key for redundancy).
   107→
   108→3. **Resource keys wrapped for teams** -- When a document or folder is shared with a team, the resource key is ECIES-wrapped for the team's public key. Any team member who can decrypt the team private key can then decrypt the resource key.
   109→
   110→4. **Role-based access** -- Roles control what actions a user can perform (admin, manager, editor, viewer). Crucially, roles are enforced at both the API level (server checks role before allowing action) and the crypto level (viewer might only receive read-only key material).
   111→
   112→5. **Device management** -- New devices generate a keypair; an existing trusted device re-encrypts the user's key material for the new device's public key. This is how Cryptomator Hub's Web of Trust model works.
   113→
   114→### Tresorit's Role Model (Industry Reference)
   115→
   116→| Role | Capabilities | Crypto Access |
   117→|---|---|---|
   118→| Owner (admin) | Full org management, billing, policy templates | Org private key |
   119→| Co-admin | User management, policy, device management (not billing) | Org private key (subset) |
   120→| Manager | Share folders, manage permissions within scope | Team private key |
   121→| Editor | Read, write, delete files/folders | Resource decryption keys |
   122→| Viewer | Read-only access | Read-only key (if separate from write key) |
   123→
   124→### Table Stakes (Team Accounts)
   125→
   126→| Feature | Why Expected | Complexity | Depends On |
   127→|---|---|---|---|
   128→| Create organization | User creates an org, becomes admin | MEDIUM | New org entity in DB, org keypair generation |
   129→| Invite members by email/identifier | Admin adds users to org | MEDIUM | Invitation flow, key re-wrapping |
   130→| Role-based permissions (admin, member, viewer) | Different access levels required | HIGH | API enforcement + crypto-level key separation |
   131→| Team/group abstraction | Group users for bulk sharing | HIGH | Team keypairs, membership management |
   132→| Remove member with key revocation | Must revoke access cryptographically, not just at API | VERY HIGH | Key rotation for all resources the removed member accessed |
   133→| Org-level storage dashboard | Admin sees aggregate usage | LOW | API aggregation queries |
   134→| Member device management | Admin can deauthorize lost devices | MEDIUM | Device registry, key re-wrapping |

   136→### Differentiators (Team Accounts)

   138→| Feature | Value Proposition | Complexity | Depends On |

   140→| Zero-knowledge org management | Admin manages org without server seeing membership relationships | VERY HIGH | Encrypted org metadata on IPFS |
   141→| Decentralized team key recovery | Team key recoverable without central authority via threshold cryptography | VERY HIGH | Shamir's secret sharing or similar |
   142→| Cryptographic role enforcement | Viewers literally cannot write because they lack the write key, not just API-blocked | HIGH | Separate read/write key hierarchy |
   143→| On-chain org identity | Org identity anchored to blockchain for auditability | MEDIUM | Smart contract integration |

   146→### Anti-Features (Team Accounts)

   148→| Anti-Feature | Why Avoid | What to Do Instead |
   149→|---|---|---|
   150→| Server-side permission enforcement only | Breaks ZK -- server could grant unauthorized access | Crypto-level key access as primary control |

   160→### How It Works for Privacy-Focused Products

   162→The challenge: accepting payment while preserving user privacy. Two tracks exist:
   163→
   164→**Track 1: Stripe (Traditional)**

   200→| Pay-per-use storage billing | Metered billing based on IPFS storage consumed | HIGH | Stripe metered billing + usage tracking |
   201→
   202→### Anti-Features (Billing)
   203→
   204→| Anti-Feature | Why Avoid | What to Do Instead |
   205→|---|---|---|
   206→| Building custom payment processing | Regulatory nightmare, PCI compliance | Use Stripe + BTCPay Server |
   207→| Enterprise sales flow (quotes, POs, net-30) | Not a demo concern | Self-service only |
   208→| Fiat invoicing for crypto payments | Complexity, legal gray area | Crypto payments are separate track, no fiat receipt |
   209→| Multiple currencies with exchange rate management | Stripe handles this automatically | Let Stripe handle currency conversion |
   210→| Refund automation | Edge cases are endless | Manual refund process via Stripe dashboard |
   211→
   212→---
   213→
   214→## Feature 4: Secure Document Signing
   215→
   216→### How It Works in Zero-Knowledge Systems
   217→
   218→Document signing in an encrypted context follows this flow:
   219→
   220→1. **Document is decrypted client-side** -- The signer decrypts the document locally.
   221→2. **Signer reviews plaintext** -- Signer sees the document content in their browser.
   222→3. **Signature is computed client-side** -- Using the signer's private key (secp256k1 from Web3Auth), the client computes a digital signature over the document hash.
   223→4. **Signature is stored alongside document** -- The signature (plus signer's public key and timestamp) is stored as metadata, encrypted and pinned to IPFS.
   224→5. **Anyone with access can verify** -- Given the document, the signature, and the signer's public key, verification is a standard ECDSA verify operation.
   225→
   226→This is fundamentally different from DocuSign/Adobe Sign where the server orchestrates signing. In a ZK system, the server never sees the document, so all signing must be client-side.
   227→
   228→### Types of Signatures
   229→
   230→| Type | Legal Weight | Implementation | Complexity |
   231→|---|---|---|---|
   232→| Electronic signature (drawn/typed) | LOW -- intent to sign | Canvas capture, stored as image | LOW |
   233→| Cryptographic digital signature | HIGH -- mathematically verifiable | ECDSA sign over document hash | MEDIUM |
   234→| Qualified electronic signature (QES) | HIGHEST -- EU eIDAS compliant | Requires certified hardware/CA | OUT OF SCOPE |
   235→
   236→**Recommendation:** Implement **cryptographic digital signatures** using the existing secp256k1 keys from Web3Auth. This is a natural fit -- every CipherBox user already has a key pair. The signature is mathematically verifiable and tied to the user's identity. Add a visual signature capture (drawn/typed) as a UX layer on top.
   237→
   238→### Table Stakes (Document Signing)
   239→
   240→| Feature | Why Expected | Complexity | Depends On |
   241→|---|---|---|---|
   242→| Sign document with private key | Core signing action | MEDIUM | Web3Auth key access, ECDSA signing |
   243→| Verify signature given public key | Anyone can check signature validity | LOW | Standard ECDSA verify |
   244→| Visual signature capture (draw/type) | Users expect to "draw" a signature | LOW | HTML Canvas signature pad |
   245→| Multi-party signing workflow | Send document for multiple signers | HIGH | Signing state machine, notification system |
   246→| Audit trail of signing events | Who signed what and when | MEDIUM | Append-only signed log |
   247→| Signed document export (PDF) | Produce a signed PDF for external use | HIGH | PDF generation with embedded signature |
   248→
   249→### Differentiators (Document Signing)
   250→
   251→| Feature | Value Proposition | Complexity | Depends On |
   252→|---|---|---|---|
   253→| IPFS-anchored signatures | Signature stored on decentralized infrastructure, tamper-evident via CID | LOW | Existing IPFS infrastructure |
   254→| Blockchain-timestamped signing | Anchor document hash on-chain for irrefutable timestamp proof | MEDIUM | Smart contract or Bitcoin OP_RETURN |
   255→| Zero-knowledge signing verification | Verify a signature exists without revealing document content | VERY HIGH | ZK-SNARK circuits |
   256→| Client-side PDF signing (PKCS#7) | Generate industry-standard signed PDFs entirely in browser | HIGH | node-signpdf or similar, X.509 cert generation |
   257→| Signature request workflow | Request signatures from other CipherBox users | MEDIUM | Notification system, signing queue |
   258→
   259→### Anti-Features (Document Signing)
   260→
   261→| Anti-Feature | Why Avoid | What to Do Instead |
   262→|---|---|---|
   263→| eIDAS/QES compliance | Requires certified CA, hardware tokens, legal framework | Cryptographic signatures with optional blockchain anchoring |
   264→| Server-side signing | Breaks ZK guarantee | All signing is client-side |
   265→| Notarization service | Legal complexity, jurisdiction-dependent | Provide timestamping as building block |
   266→| Signing for non-CipherBox users | Requires external key management | Limit to CipherBox-to-CipherBox signing |
   267→| Template-based signing (fill-and-sign forms) | DocuSeal territory, massive scope | Simple "sign this document" flow only |
   268→
   269→---
   270→
   271→## Feature Dependencies
   272→
   273→### Dependency Map
   274→
   275→```text
   276→M1/M2 Prerequisites:
   277→  File sharing (M2) -----> Document sharing (same key-wrapping pattern)
   278→  Encryption core (M1) --> Document encryption (same AES-256-GCM)
   279→  IPFS storage (M1) -----> Document persistence on IPFS
   280→  Web3Auth keys (M1) ----> Digital signature key material
   281→
   282→M3 Internal Dependencies:
   283→  Team Accounts ---------> Team document sharing
   284→  Team Accounts ---------> Team billing (org pays for seats)
   285→  Encrypted Docs --------> Document signing (need a document to sign)
   286→  Billing ---------------> Storage quotas (need billing to enforce limits)
   287→
   288→Build Order (recommended):
   289→  1. Billing (enables free/paid tiers, gates everything else)
   290→  2. Team Accounts (enables org-level features)
   291→  3. Encrypted Docs (largest effort, most visible feature)
   292→  4. Document Signing (builds on docs + keys, lowest standalone value)
   293→```
   294→
   295→### Dependency on M2 Features
   296→
   297→| M2 Feature | M3 Usage |
   298→|---|---|
   299→| File/folder sharing (ECIES re-wrapping) | Document sharing uses identical pattern |
   300→| File versioning (CID retention) | Document version history |
   301→| Encrypted search | Search within documents (stretch goal) |
   302→| Web3Auth MFA | Required for signing key security |
   303→
   304→---
   305→
   306→## Complexity Summary
   307→
   308→| Feature Area | Estimated Effort | Risk Level | Notes |
   309→|---|---|---|---|

   317→| Document signing (basic) | 2-4 weeks | LOW | ECDSA sign/verify, UI for signature capture |
   318→| Document signing (multi-party) | 4-6 weeks | MEDIUM | State machine, notification flow |
   319→| Document signing (PDF export) | 3-5 weeks | MEDIUM | Client-side PDF generation with embedded sig |
   320→
   321→**Total estimated effort for full M3:** 40-80+ weeks, depending on scope.
   322→
   323→**Recommended MVP scope:** Rich text docs + basic teams + Stripe billing + basic signing = 14-23 weeks.
   324→
   325→---
   326→
   327→## MVP Recommendation
   328→
   329→### Build First (Phase 1 of M3)

   334→
   335→3. **Encrypted rich text editor** -- Yjs + SecSync + TipTap. Single-user editing first, then real-time collaboration. This is the flagship feature. 6-10 weeks.
   336→
   337→4. **Basic document signing** -- ECDSA signature using existing Web3Auth keys. Visual signature pad. Single-signer flow. 2-4 weeks.
   338→
   339→### Defer to Phase 2 of M3

   348→### Explicitly Skip (Not for a Tech Demo)

   355→
   356→---
   357→
   358→## Competitor Feature Matrix
   359→
   360→| Feature | CryptPad | Tresorit | Proton Docs | Skiff (defunct) | Standard Notes |

   362→| Encrypted docs | Yes (ChainPad) | No (storage only) | Yes (Yjs-based) | Yes (Yjs) | Yes (notes only) |

   372→| IPFS storage | No | No | No | No | No |
   373→
   374→**CipherBox differentiators:** IPFS-backed storage, cryptographic document signing with Web3Auth keys, anonymous crypto payments, and decentralized architecture set CipherBox apart from every competitor listed above. No existing product combines encrypted editing with decentralized storage and cryptographic signing.

1→# Technology Stack: Milestone 3
     2→
     3→**Project:** CipherBox - Encrypted Productivity Suite
     4→**Researched:** 2026-02-11
     5→**Scope:** Document/Spreadsheet/Presentation editors, Team accounts, Billing, Document signing
     6→
     7→## Executive Summary
     8→
     9→M3 transforms CipherBox from encrypted file storage into an encrypted productivity suite.
    10→The core constraint remains: all content is client-side encrypted and the server never sees
    11→plaintext. This constrains every technology choice -- editors must operate entirely in-browser
    12→on decrypted content, collaboration must use E2EE CRDTs (not server-mediated OT), and document
    13→signing must work with client-side cryptographic primitives.
    14→
    15→The recommended stack centers on TipTap 3.x (rich text), Univer (spreadsheets), a custom
    16→TipTap-based slide editor (presentations), CASL (authorization), Stripe + NOWPayments
    17→(billing), and LibPDF + Web Crypto (document signing).
    18→
    19→---
    20→
    21→## 1. Document Editor (Rich Text)
    22→
    23→### Recommended: TipTap 3.x + Yjs
    24→
    25→| Package | Version | Purpose |
    26→|---------|---------|---------|
    27→| `@tiptap/react` | ^3.19.0 | React integration for TipTap editor |
    28→| `@tiptap/starter-kit` | ^3.19.0 | Bundle of essential extensions (bold, italic, lists, etc.) |
    29→| `@tiptap/extension-collaboration` | ^3.19.0 | Yjs-based CRDT collaboration |
    30→| `@tiptap/extension-collaboration-cursor` | ^3.19.0 | Shared cursor awareness |
    31→| `@tiptap/extension-table` | ^3.19.0 | Table editing support |
    32→| `@tiptap/extension-image` | ^3.19.0 | Inline image support |
    33→| `@tiptap/extension-placeholder` | ^3.19.0 | Placeholder text |
    34→| `@tiptap/extension-text-align` | ^3.19.0 | Text alignment |
    35→| `@tiptap/extension-underline` | ^3.19.0 | Underline formatting |
    36→| `@tiptap/extension-color` | ^3.19.0 | Text color |
    37→| `@tiptap/extension-highlight` | ^3.19.0 | Text highlighting |
    38→| `yjs` | ^13.x | CRDT data structure for conflict-free sync |
    39→| `y-indexeddb` | ^9.x | Offline persistence for Yjs documents |
    40→
    41→**Confidence:** HIGH -- TipTap 3.0 is stable (confirmed Feb 2026), actively maintained, and
    42→the de facto standard for React rich text editors.
    43→
    44→**Why TipTap over alternatives:**
    45→
    46→| Editor | Why Not |
    47→|--------|---------|
    48→| Slate.js | Lower-level API, more work to build equivalent UX. No built-in collaboration. |
    49→| Quill | Older architecture, less extensible, weaker TypeScript support. |
    50→| Lexical (Meta) | Newer but smaller extension ecosystem. Less community adoption for production apps. |
    51→| CKEditor 5 | Proprietary collaboration server. GPL license requires open-sourcing derivative work. |
    52→| ProseMirror (raw) | TipTap IS ProseMirror with a better DX layer. No reason to go lower. |
    53→
    54→**Zero-knowledge architecture fit:**
    55→
    56→TipTap + Yjs is uniquely suited for CipherBox because:
    57→
    58→1. Yjs is a CRDT -- it does not require a central server to mediate changes (unlike OT).
    59→2. Yjs document state is a binary blob (`Y.encodeStateAsUpdate()`) that can be
    60→   AES-256-GCM encrypted before storage/transmission.
    61→3. The Yjs E2EE pattern is documented and used in production (Proton Docs uses Yjs with E2EE).
    62→4. Offline-first: y-indexeddb persists the encrypted Yjs doc locally; sync happens
    63→   when peers reconnect.
    64→
    65→**Integration with existing stack:**
    66→
    67→- Yjs doc binary is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a per-document `fileKey` (same
    68→  pattern as existing file encryption).
    69→- Encrypted Yjs state is stored as an IPFS blob (same as files).
    70→- Document metadata (name, type, lastModified) lives in the folder IPNS record.
    71→- No server-side changes needed for basic single-user editing. Team collaboration
    72→  requires a thin WebSocket relay (see Architecture note below).
    73→
    74→### Collaboration Relay (for team editing)
    75→
    76→| Package | Version | Purpose |
    77→|---------|---------|---------|
    78→| `@hocuspocus/server` | ^3.4.4 | WebSocket server for Yjs sync |
    79→| `@hocuspocus/provider` | ^3.4.4 | Client-side WebSocket provider for Yjs |
    80→
    81→**Architecture note:** For team collaboration, Hocuspocus acts as a *dumb relay*. It forwards
    82→encrypted Yjs update blobs between connected clients. The server never decrypts content.
    83→Clients decrypt updates using the shared document key (distributed via ECIES re-wrapping,
    84→same as M2 file sharing). Hocuspocus hooks validate authentication and authorization but
    85→never touch plaintext.
    86→
    87→---
    88→
    89→## 2. Spreadsheet Editor
    90→
    91→### Recommended: Univer Sheets
    92→
    93→| Package | Version | Purpose |
    94→|---------|---------|---------|
    95→| `@univerjs/core` | ^0.15.x | Core engine |
    96→| `@univerjs/design` | ^0.15.x | Design system / theming |
    97→| `@univerjs/engine-render` | ^0.15.x | Canvas rendering engine |
    98→| `@univerjs/engine-formula` | ^0.15.x | Formula calculation engine |
    99→| `@univerjs/sheets` | ^0.15.x | Spreadsheet data model |
   100→| `@univerjs/sheets-ui` | ^0.15.x | Spreadsheet UI components |
   101→| `@univerjs/sheets-formula` | ^0.15.x | Formula integration |
   102→| `@univerjs/sheets-formula-ui` | ^0.15.x | Formula bar UI |
   103→| `@univerjs/sheets-numfmt` | ^0.15.x | Number formatting |
   104→| `@univerjs/sheets-numfmt-ui` | ^0.15.x | Number format UI |
   105→| `@univerjs/docs` | ^0.15.x | Required dependency for cell editing |
   106→| `@univerjs/docs-ui` | ^0.15.x | Required dependency for cell editing |
   107→| `@univerjs/ui` | ^0.15.x | Generic UI framework |
   108→
   109→**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- Univer is the most capable open-source spreadsheet framework but
   110→is still pre-1.0 (0.15.x). APIs may change between minor versions. However, it is actively
   111→maintained with releases every few days.
   112→
   113→**Why Univer over alternatives:**
   114→
   115→| Library | Why Not |
   116→|---------|---------|
   117→| FortuneSheet | Smaller community, fewer features (no conditional formatting, limited formulas). |
   118→| Handsontable | Commercial license required for production. Not truly open source. |
   119→| react-spreadsheet | Too simple -- no formula engine, no formatting, no charts. Data grid, not spreadsheet. |
   120→| AG Grid | Data grid, not spreadsheet. No formula bar, cell merging, etc. |
   121→| Jspreadsheet CE | jQuery-era architecture, weak TypeScript support. |
   122→
   123→**Zero-knowledge architecture fit:**
   124→
   125→- Univer operates entirely client-side. The spreadsheet data model is a JSON structure
   126→  that can be serialized, encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and stored as an IPFS blob.
   127→- `JSON.stringify(univerInstance.save())` produces the complete spreadsheet state.
   128→- On load: fetch encrypted blob from IPFS, decrypt, `JSON.parse()`, hydrate Univer.
   129→- Formula computation happens client-side -- server never needs access.
   130→
   131→**Collaboration caveat:**
   132→
   133→Univer's built-in collaboration uses OT (Operational Transformation), which requires a
   134→server to mediate. This conflicts with CipherBox's zero-knowledge model. For M3, recommend
   135→**single-user editing only** for spreadsheets. Multi-user spreadsheet collaboration would
   136→require either:
   137→
   138→- Building a Yjs binding for Univer (significant effort, no existing solution)
   139→- Using Univer's OT in a TEE enclave (complex, possibly over-engineered for a demo)
   140→
   141→**Recommendation:** Ship spreadsheets as single-user-editable in M3. If team spreadsheet
   142→editing becomes a priority, evaluate building a Yjs adapter in a future milestone.
   143→
   144→---
   145→
   146→## 3. Presentation Editor (Slides)
   147→
   148→### Recommended: Custom TipTap-based Slide Editor
   149→
   150→There is no mature, open-source, React-native slide editor comparable to Google Slides.
   151→The best approach for CipherBox is to build a slide editor using TipTap as the per-slide
   152→content editor, with a custom slide deck wrapper.
   153→
   154→**Approach:**
   155→
   156→| Component | Technology | Purpose |
   157→|-----------|-----------|---------|
   158→| Per-slide content | TipTap 3.x (same as doc editor) | Rich text, images, shapes per slide |
   159→| Slide deck model | Custom React + Zustand | Slide ordering, transitions, themes |
   160→| Slide thumbnails | `html2canvas` or DOM snapshots | Preview panel |
   161→| Export to PPTX | `pptxgenjs` ^3.x | PowerPoint export |
   162→
   163→| Package | Version | Purpose |
   164→|---------|---------|---------|
   165→| `pptxgenjs` | ^3.12.0 | PPTX file generation for export |
   166→| `html2canvas` | ^1.4.1 | DOM-to-canvas for slide thumbnails |
   167→
   168→**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- This is a custom build, not an off-the-shelf solution. Gamma.app
   169→(a YC-backed startup) built their presentation editor on ProseMirror/TipTap, proving the
   170→approach works. But there is no open-source version to drop in.
   171→
   172→**Why NOT use existing presentation libraries:**
   173→
   174→| Library | Why Not |
   175→|---------|---------|
   176→| reveal.js | Presentation *viewer/player*, not an *editor*. No WYSIWYG editing UI. |
   177→| Spectacle | Code-based slide authoring (JSX). Not a visual editor. |
   178→| Slidev | Markdown-based, developer-focused. Not a visual editor. |
   179→| PptxGenJS | File *generation* only. No editing UI. |
   180→
   181→**Zero-knowledge architecture fit:**
   182→
   183→- Each slide deck is a JSON structure: `{ slides: [{ content: TipTapJSON, layout, theme }] }`.
   184→- Encrypted and stored as a single IPFS blob (same as documents).
   185→- Collaboration uses same Yjs approach as documents (one Y.Doc per slide deck).
   186→
   187→**Scope recommendation for demo:** Focus on basic slide editing (text, images, backgrounds,
   188→simple layouts). Do NOT attempt animations, transitions, or complex shape editing. That
   189→is a multi-year effort for dedicated teams.
   190→
   191→---
   192→
   193→## 4. Team Accounts and Authorization
   194→
   195→### Recommended: CASL + Custom NestJS Guards
   196→
   197→| Package | Version | Side | Purpose |
   198→|---------|---------|------|---------|
   199→| `@casl/ability` | ^6.7.5 | Shared | Define and check permissions |
   200→| `@casl/react` | ^4.0.0 | Frontend | React components for conditional rendering |
   201→| `nest-casl` | ^1.9.15 | Backend | NestJS integration for CASL |
   202→
   203→**Confidence:** HIGH -- CASL is the standard authorization library for the Node.js/NestJS
   204→ecosystem. Well-documented, actively maintained, and explicitly designed for RBAC/ABAC.
   205→
   206→**Why CASL over alternatives:**
   207→
   208→| Alternative | Why Not |
   209→|-------------|---------|
   210→| Custom guards only | Reinventing the wheel. CASL provides a proven, testable abstraction. |
   211→| casbin | More complex (policy language), designed for microservices. Overkill for CipherBox. |
   212→| NestJS built-in roles | Too simple. No field-level permissions, no conditions, no client-side sharing. |
   213→
   214→**Role model for CipherBox teams:**
   215→
   216→| Role | Permissions |
   217→|------|------------|
   218→| `owner` | All operations, billing, member management, delete org |
   219→| `admin` | All operations except billing and org deletion |
   220→| `member` | Create, read, update, delete own files. Read shared files. |
   221→| `viewer` | Read-only access to shared files/folders |
   222→
   223→**Database additions (TypeORM entities):**
   224→
   225→```text
   226→Organization { id, name, createdAt, updatedAt }
   227→OrganizationMember { orgId, userId, role, invitedAt, joinedAt }
   228→OrganizationInvite { orgId, email, role, token, expiresAt }
   229→```
   230→
   231→**Zero-knowledge implications:**
   232→
   233→Team key management extends M2's sharing model:
   234→
   235→- Each organization has an `orgFolderKey` encrypted to each member's public key (ECIES).
   236→- When a member is added, the org owner re-wraps the `orgFolderKey` to the new member's
   237→  public key.
   238→- When a member is removed, key rotation is triggered: new `orgFolderKey`, re-encrypt
   239→  all org folder metadata, re-wrap to remaining members.
   240→- The server stores encrypted keys only. It enforces role-based API access but never
   241→  sees plaintext content.
   242→
   243→---
   244→
   245→## 5. Billing Integration
   246→
   247→### 5A. Stripe (Traditional Payments)
   248→
   249→| Package | Version | Side | Purpose |
   250→|---------|---------|------|---------|
   251→| `stripe` | ^20.3.1 | Backend | Stripe API SDK |
   252→| `@golevelup/nestjs-stripe` | ^0.9.3 | Backend | NestJS module with webhook autowiring |
   253→| `@stripe/stripe-js` | ^5.x | Frontend | Stripe.js loader |
   254→| `@stripe/react-stripe-js` | ^5.6.0 | Frontend | React Elements components |
   255→
   256→**Confidence:** HIGH -- Stripe is the industry standard. The NestJS integration via
   257→`@golevelup/nestjs-stripe` handles webhook verification and routing automatically.
   258→
   259→**Integration approach:**
   260→
   261→- Use Stripe Checkout (hosted payment page) for initial subscriptions. Minimizes PCI scope.
   262→- Use Stripe Customer Portal for subscription management (upgrade, downgrade, cancel).
   263→- Webhook handler processes `checkout.session.completed`, `invoice.paid`,
   264→  `customer.subscription.updated`, `customer.subscription.deleted`.
   265→- Store `stripeCustomerId` and `stripeSubscriptionId` on the User/Organization entity.
   266→- Feature gating: check subscription tier in NestJS guards alongside CASL permissions.
   267→
   268→**Database additions:**
   269→
   270→```text
   271→Subscription { id, orgId, stripeCustomerId, stripeSubscriptionId, tier, status, currentPeriodEnd }
   272→```
   273→
   274→### 5B. Crypto Payments (Privacy-Preserving)
   275→
   276→| Package | Version | Side | Purpose |
   277→|---------|---------|------|---------|
   278→| `@nowpaymentsio/nowpayments-api-js` | ^1.0.x | Backend | NOWPayments API client |
   279→
   280→**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- NOWPayments is a legitimate service with an official npm package,
   281→but the package is less actively maintained than Stripe's SDK.
   282→
   283→**Why NOWPayments over alternatives:**
   284→
   285→| Alternative | Why Not |
   286→|-------------|---------|
   287→| BTCPay Server | Requires self-hosting a Bitcoin full node. Heavy infrastructure for a demo. |
   288→| CoinGate | Similar to NOWPayments but smaller JS ecosystem. |
   289→| Direct Web3 (ethers.js) | Requires building your own payment tracking, exchange rate handling, confirmation logic. |
   290→| Coinbase Commerce | Coinbase is a centralized exchange -- undermines anonymity goal. |
   291→
   292→**Why NOWPayments:**
   293→
   294→- Hosted service -- no infrastructure to manage.
   295→- Supports 350+ cryptocurrencies including BTC, ETH, USDT, USDC.
   296→- REST API with IPN (Instant Payment Notification) webhooks.
   297→- No KYC required for the payer (preserves anonymity).
   298→- 1% fee (competitive with crypto payment processors).
   299→
   300→**Integration approach:**
   301→
   302→- Create a payment invoice via NOWPayments API when user selects crypto payment.
   303→- Display payment address and QR code to user.
   304→- Backend receives IPN webhook when payment is confirmed.
   305→- Map payment to subscription activation (same tier system as Stripe).
   306→- Crypto payments activate a fixed-duration subscription (e.g., 30 days per payment).
   307→
   308→**Alternative consideration: BTCPay Server**
   309→
   310→If the project later needs maximum decentralization (no third-party payment processor),
   311→BTCPay Server is the gold standard. It is self-hosted, open-source, and zero-fee. However,
   312→it requires running a Bitcoin full node (~500GB disk) and optional Lightning node. This
   313→is too heavy for a demo but worth noting for a production roadmap.
   314→
   315→---
   316→
   317→## 6. Secure Document Signing
   318→
   319→### Recommended: LibPDF + Web Crypto API + react-signature-canvas
   320→
   321→| Package | Version | Side | Purpose |
   322→|---------|---------|------|---------|
   323→| `@libpdf/core` | latest (beta) | Shared | PDF parsing, modification, digital signatures |
   324→| `react-signature-canvas` | ^1.0.7 | Frontend | Signature drawing pad |
   325→| `@signpdf/signpdf` | ^3.3.0 | Backend (optional) | PDF signing with certificates |
   326→
   327→**Confidence:** MEDIUM-LOW for LibPDF (beta, APIs may change), HIGH for the overall approach.
   328→
   329→**Why LibPDF over alternatives:**
   330→
   331→| Alternative | Why Not |
   332→|-------------|---------|
   333→| pdf-lib | Last updated 4 years ago (v1.17.1). No digital signature support. No active maintenance. |
   334→| Apryse/Nutrient | Commercial. Expensive licensing. |
   335→| node-signpdf (@signpdf/signpdf) | Good for server-side signing but CipherBox needs client-side signing. |
   336→
   337→**Why LibPDF:**
   338→
   339→- TypeScript-first (designed for TS, not retrofitted).
   340→- Supports PAdES digital signatures (B-B through B-LTA).
   341→- Preserves existing digital signatures during modification (incremental saves).
   342→- Works in both Node.js and the browser from the same code.
   343→- Built by Documenso (the open-source DocuSign alternative) -- real production usage.
   344→- Under active development with frequent releases.
   345→
   346→**Zero-knowledge document signing approach:**
   347→
   348→CipherBox document signing is fundamentally different from DocuSign because documents
   349→are encrypted. The signing flow:
   350→
   351→1. User opens encrypted document in browser (decrypted client-side).
   352→2. User draws signature on `react-signature-canvas` or types/uploads signature image.
   353→3. Client generates a signing keypair (or uses their Web3Auth-derived key).
   354→4. Client creates a cryptographic signature over the document hash using Web Crypto API
   355→   (`crypto.subtle.sign` with ECDSA P-256 or the existing secp256k1 key).
   356→5. The signature + signer's public key + timestamp are embedded in a signature metadata
   357→   record stored alongside the document.
   358→6. For PDF export: LibPDF embeds the digital signature into a rendered PDF.
   359→7. Verification: any party with the signer's public key can verify the signature
   360→   against the document hash.
   361→
   362→**Important distinction:** This is a *cryptographic* signature (proving the signer had
   363→the private key), not just a visual e-signature overlay. CipherBox's existing key
   364→infrastructure (secp256k1 via Web3Auth) makes this natural.
   365→
   366→**Database additions:**
   367→
   368→```text
   369→DocumentSignature { id, documentId, signerPublicKey, signatureHex, documentHash, signedAt, metadata }
   370→SignatureRequest { id, documentId, requesterId, signerEmail, status, expiresAt }
   371→```
   372→
   373→---
   374→
   375→## 7. Supporting Infrastructure
   376→
   377→### WebSocket Server (for collaboration relay)
   378→
   379→The existing NestJS backend should be extended with a WebSocket gateway for Hocuspocus.
   380→
   381→| Package | Version | Side | Purpose |
   382→|---------|---------|------|---------|
   383→| `@nestjs/websockets` | ^11.x | Backend | NestJS WebSocket support |
   384→| `@nestjs/platform-ws` | ^11.x | Backend | WS adapter for NestJS |
   385→
   386→**Note:** Hocuspocus can run as a standalone process or be integrated into the NestJS
   387→application. For CipherBox, running it as a separate process behind the same reverse proxy
   388→is recommended to isolate long-lived WebSocket connections from the REST API.
   389→
   390→### Email (for invitations and signature requests)
   391→
   392→| Package | Version | Side | Purpose |
   393→|---------|---------|------|---------|
   394→| `@nestjs-modules/mailer` | ^2.x | Backend | NestJS email integration |
   395→| `nodemailer` | ^6.x | Backend | Email transport (peer dep of mailer) |
   396→
   397→**Note:** Required for team invitations and signature request notifications. Use a
   398→transactional email service (Resend, SendGrid, or AWS SES) as the transport.
   399→
   400→---
   401→
   402→## What NOT to Add
   403→
   404→| Technology | Why Not |
   405→|------------|---------|
   406→| Socket.IO | Hocuspocus uses native WebSockets via `ws`. Adding Socket.IO would duplicate functionality. |
   407→| MongoDB | Document editors do not need a separate document database. Yjs state is stored as encrypted blobs on IPFS. Relational metadata stays in PostgreSQL. |
   408→| Redis Pub/Sub for collab | Hocuspocus handles multi-instance sync natively. BullMQ + Redis already exists for job queues. |
   409→| GraphQL | REST + OpenAPI (existing pattern) is sufficient. GraphQL adds complexity without clear benefit for CipherBox's API surface. |
   410→| Electron | Tauri v2 is already chosen for desktop. Do not add Electron. |
   411→| Firebase/Supabase Realtime | Third-party real-time databases conflict with zero-knowledge architecture. |
   412→| OT-based collaboration | Requires server to see document structure. Incompatible with E2EE. Use CRDTs (Yjs). |
   413→
   414→---

   435→

1→# M3 Architecture: Productivity Suite Integration
     2→
     3→**Domain:** Encrypted document editing, team accounts, billing, document signing
     4→**Researched:** 2026-02-11
     5→**Confidence:** MEDIUM (editor integration is novel territory; billing and team patterns are well-established)
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Table of Contents
    10→
    11→1. [Existing Architecture Summary](#1-existing-architecture-summary)
    12→2. [Document Editors](#2-document-editors)
    13→3. [Team Accounts](#3-team-accounts)
    14→4. [Billing and Payments](#4-billing-and-payments)
    15→5. [Document Signing](#5-document-signing)
    16→6. [New Database Entities](#6-new-database-entities)
    17→7. [Component Boundary Map](#7-component-boundary-map)
    18→8. [Data Flow Changes](#8-data-flow-changes)
    19→9. [Real-Time Collaboration Assessment](#9-real-time-collaboration-assessment)
    20→10. [Suggested Build Order](#10-suggested-build-order)
    21→11. [Sources](#11-sources)
    22→
    23→---
    24→
    25→## 1. Existing Architecture Summary
    26→
    27→Before detailing M3 additions, here is the current system as of M1/M2 completion.
    28→
    29→### Current Components
    30→
    31→| Component | Technology | Role |
    32→|-----------|-----------|------|
    33→| Web App | React 18 + Zustand + Vite | File browser, auth, upload/download, IPNS sync |
    34→| API | NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL | Auth, vault, IPFS/IPNS relay, TEE coordination |
    35→| Desktop | Tauri v2 + Rust FUSE | Transparent encrypted filesystem mount |
    36→| IPFS | Pinata (managed pinning) | Encrypted content storage |
    37→| IPNS | Per-folder Ed25519 keypairs | Mutable metadata pointers |
    38→| TEE | Phala Cloud / AWS Nitro | IPNS auto-republishing |
    39→| Auth | Web3Auth + SIWE | Key derivation and identity |
    40→
    41→### Key Constraints Preserved in M3
    42→
    43→1. **Zero-knowledge server** -- the backend NEVER sees plaintext content or unencrypted keys
    44→2. **Client-side encryption** -- all crypto operations happen in-browser or in-desktop
    45→3. **Per-folder IPNS** -- each folder has its own Ed25519 keypair and AES-256 folder key
    46→4. **ECIES key wrapping** -- all symmetric keys wrapped with user's secp256k1 public key
    47→
    48→### By M3, These M2 Features Exist
    49→
    50→- File/folder sharing via ECIES re-wrapping (shared folder keys re-encrypted to recipient's public key)
    51→- File versioning (version chains stored in folder metadata)
    52→- Client-side search (encrypted index)
    53→- MFA support
    54→
    55→---
    56→
    57→## 2. Document Editors
    58→
    59→### 2.1 Problem Statement
    60→
    61→CipherBox stores encrypted files on IPFS. Currently, editing requires download, decrypt, edit in external app, re-encrypt, re-upload. M3 adds in-browser editing for documents, spreadsheets, and presentations -- while preserving zero-knowledge.
    62→
    63→### 2.2 Architecture Decision: Decrypt-Edit-Encrypt Pipeline
    64→
    65→The fundamental pattern for all editors is:
    66→
    67→```
    68→1. User opens file in CipherBox
    69→2. Client fetches encrypted blob from IPFS via backend relay
    70→3. Client decrypts with file's AES-256-GCM key
    71→4. Decrypted content loaded into in-browser editor component
    72→5. User edits in the editor (all in-browser, all in RAM)
    73→6. On save: editor exports content -> client encrypts -> uploads to IPFS -> updates IPNS metadata
    74→7. Old CID unpinned
    75→```
    76→
    77→This is architecturally identical to the existing "update file" flow (DATA_FLOWS.md section 6.5) but with the editor replacing the download/re-upload step.
    78→
    79→### 2.3 Editor Technology Recommendations
    80→
    81→#### Rich Text / Documents: Tiptap (built on ProseMirror)
    82→
    83→**Recommendation: Tiptap v2+**
    84→
    85→| Criterion | Tiptap | CKEditor 5 | Quill |
    86→|-----------|--------|------------|-------|
    87→| React integration | Native (@tiptap/react) | Adapter needed | React-Quill wrapper |
    88→| Content format | JSON (ProseMirror doc) | Custom model | Delta JSON |
    89→| Headless / unstyled | Yes (matches existing UI) | No (opinionated UI) | Partial |
    90→| Collaboration support | Yjs plugin (optional, future) | Proprietary | Limited |
    91→| License | MIT (core) | GPL (open) or commercial | BSD |
    92→| Bundle size | Modular, ~50KB base | ~300KB+ | ~40KB |
    93→
    94→**Why Tiptap:**
    95→
    96→- Headless architecture -- CipherBox can style the editor to match existing UI
    97→- JSON export via `editor.getJSON()` maps cleanly to encrypt-and-store
    98→- ProseMirror schema enforcement prevents invalid document structures
    99→- Yjs integration available for future real-time collaboration (M4+)
   100→- MIT licensed core is compatible with CipherBox
   101→
   102→**Content format:** Tiptap's ProseMirror JSON document is the "file format" for CipherBox documents. This JSON is what gets AES-256-GCM encrypted and stored on IPFS.
   103→
   104→```typescript
   105→// Save flow (simplified)
   106→const docJson = editor.getJSON();
   107→const plaintext = new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(docJson));
   108→const fileKey = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32));
   109→const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12));
   110→const ciphertext = await aesGcmEncrypt(plaintext, fileKey, iv);
   111→// Upload ciphertext to IPFS, wrap fileKey with ECIES, update IPNS
   112→```

   203→## 3. Team Accounts
   204→
   205→### 3.1 Architecture Decision: Shared Team Vaults with Per-Team Key Hierarchy
   206→
   207→Following the patterns established by Keeper and Bitwarden for zero-knowledge team vaults.
   208→
   209→### 3.2 Key Hierarchy Extension
   210→
   211→Current key hierarchy (per-user):
   212→
   213→```
   214→User ECDSA Keypair (secp256k1)
   215→  -> rootFolderKey (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   216→    -> folderKey per folder (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   217→      -> fileKey per file (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   218→```
   219→
   220→Extended hierarchy for teams:
   221→
   222→```
   223→Team
   224→  -> teamKey (AES-256, randomly generated on team creation)
   225→    -> teamFolderKey per shared folder (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to... what?)
   226→
   227→Each team member gets:
   228→  -> encryptedTeamKey = ECIES(teamKey, memberPublicKey)
   229→    stored in team_members table
   230→```
   231→
   232→**How it works:**
   233→
   234→1. Team creator generates a random `teamKey` (AES-256)
   235→2. Creator encrypts `teamKey` with their own `publicKey` and stores it
   236→3. When inviting a member, creator decrypts `teamKey` client-side, then re-encrypts with invitee's `publicKey`
   237→4. Team folders use `teamKey` as the root -- subfolder keys and file keys within team folders are ECIES-wrapped to each member's `publicKey` OR encrypted with `teamKey`
   238→
   239→**Design decision: Wrap to teamKey, not individual publicKeys**
   240→
   241→For team folders, file keys and folder keys should be encrypted with the `teamKey` rather than individual member public keys. This means:
   242→
   243→- Adding a team member = re-encrypt `teamKey` to their public key (one operation)
   244→- Removing a team member = rotate `teamKey` and re-encrypt to remaining members (heavier, but necessary for security)
   245→- Files in team folders encrypted with keys derived from `teamKey`, not per-member
   246→
   247→This matches the Keeper/Bitwarden model and avoids the O(members x files) key re-wrapping problem.
   248→
   249→### 3.3 Permission Model
   250→
   251→```typescript
   252→type TeamRole = 'owner' | 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
   253→
   254→// Capabilities per role
   255→const ROLE_PERMISSIONS = {
   256→  owner: ['read', 'write', 'delete', 'manage_members', 'manage_team', 'billing'],
   257→  admin: ['read', 'write', 'delete', 'manage_members'],
   258→  editor: ['read', 'write'],
   259→  viewer: ['read'],
   260→} as const;
   261→```
   262→
   263→**Permission enforcement:**
   264→
   265→- **Server-side:** Team membership and role checked on all team-scoped API calls
   266→- **Client-side:** UI hides actions the user's role does not permit
   267→- **Crypto-level:** Viewers receive `teamKey` (read access means decrypt access -- cannot be revoked cryptographically without key rotation)
   268→
   269→**Important caveat:** In a zero-knowledge system, read access = possession of decryption key. A viewer who has been removed can still decrypt previously-accessed content. Revoking access requires rotating the `teamKey` and re-encrypting all team folder content. This is an inherent limitation of client-side encryption architectures.
   270→
   271→### 3.4 Team IPNS Architecture
   272→
   273→Team folders need their own IPNS keypairs, just like user folders. The difference is the IPNS private key management:
   274→
   275→- Team folder's `ipnsPrivateKey` is encrypted with `teamKey` (not individual member's public key)
   276→- Any team member with `editor` or higher role can decrypt `teamKey`, then decrypt `ipnsPrivateKey`, then sign IPNS updates
   277→- TEE republishing for team folders: `encryptedIpnsPrivateKey` is still encrypted with TEE public key (unchanged)
   278→

   482→## 5. Document Signing
   483→
   484→### 5.1 Architecture Decision: Cryptographic Signatures with CipherBox Keys
   485→
   486→CipherBox users already have secp256k1 ECDSA keypairs (from Web3Auth). These can produce digital signatures that are cryptographically verifiable. However, these are NOT legally binding qualified electronic signatures (QES) under eIDAS without certificate authority backing.
   487→
   488→### 5.2 Signature Levels
   489→
   490→| Level | CipherBox Support | Legal Standing |
   491→|-------|-------------------|---------------|
   492→| Simple Electronic Signature (SES) | Yes -- intent captured, signature stored | Legally recognized in most jurisdictions |
   493→| Advanced Electronic Signature (AES) | Partially -- uniquely linked to signer via secp256k1 key, but no qualified certificate | Recognized with higher evidentiary value |
   494→| Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) | No -- requires qualified certificate from QTSP | Equivalent to handwritten signature in EU |
   495→
   496→**Recommendation for M3:** Implement SES/AES-level signing using existing secp256k1 keys. QES requires integration with a Qualified Trust Service Provider (QTSP) and is out of scope for a technology demonstrator.
   497→
   498→### 5.3 Signing Flow
   499→
   500→```
   501→1. User opens document to sign
   502→2. Client decrypts document content
   503→3. Client computes SHA-256 hash of plaintext content
   504→4. Client signs hash with user's secp256k1 privateKey:
   505→   signature = ECDSA_sign(SHA256(content), privateKey)
   506→5. Signature metadata stored in folder metadata alongside file entry:
   507→   {
   508→     signerPublicKey: "0x04abc...",
   509→     signatureHex: "0xdef...",
   510→     contentHash: "sha256:abc123...",
   511→     signedAt: 1707000000,
   512→     signedCid: "QmXxx..."  // CID of the content that was signed
   513→   }
   514→6. Signature metadata encrypted with folderKey (part of IPNS metadata)
   515→7. Verification: any user with folder access can verify signature
   516→   matches publicKey and content hash
   517→```
   518→
   519→### 5.4 Verification Properties
   520→
   521→- **Integrity:** SHA-256 content hash ensures signed content has not been modified
   522→- **Non-repudiation:** ECDSA signature proves the holder of the private key signed
   523→- **Timestamp:** `signedAt` provides temporal evidence (not cryptographic timestamp -- would need TSA for that)
   524→- **Auditability:** The `signedCid` links the signature to a specific IPFS CID
   525→
   526→### 5.5 Multi-Signer Support
   527→
   528→For documents requiring multiple signatures (e.g., contracts):
   529→
   530→```typescript
   531→type SignatureRecord = {
   532→  signerPublicKey: string;
   533→  signatureHex: string;
   534→  contentHash: string;
   535→  signedAt: number;
   536→  signedCid: string;
   537→};
   538→
   539→// In file entry metadata
   540→type SignableFileEntry = FileEntry & {
   541→  signatures?: SignatureRecord[];
   542→  requiredSigners?: string[];  // publicKeys of required signers
   543→  signatureStatus?: 'pending' | 'partial' | 'complete';
   544→};
   545→```
   546→
   547→### 5.6 Integration Points
   548→
   549→| Existing Component | Change |
   550→|-------------------|--------|
   551→| Folder metadata schema | Add `signatures` array to file entries |
   552→| `apps/web/src/services/file-crypto.service.ts` | Add signing and verification functions |
   553→| `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/FileListItem.tsx` | Show signature status icon |
   554→| New: `apps/web/src/components/signing/SignaturePanel.tsx` | UI for signing and viewing signatures |
   555→| New: `apps/web/src/components/signing/VerifySignature.tsx` | Verification results display |
   556→| New: `apps/web/src/services/signing.service.ts` | ECDSA signing/verification logic |
   557→
   558→### 5.7 What This Is NOT
   559→
   560→- NOT a replacement for DocuSign/Adobe Sign (no legal compliance framework)
   561→- NOT QES (no qualified certificates)
   562→- NOT timestamped by a TSA (trusted timestamping authority)
   563→- IS a cryptographic proof that a specific key holder approved specific content at a claimed time
   564→- IS verifiable by any party with the signer's public key

   612→    billing.service.ts
   613→    stripe/
   614→      stripe.service.ts
   615→      stripe-webhook.controller.ts
   616→    crypto/
   617→      nowpayments.service.ts
   618→      nowpayments-webhook.controller.ts
   619→    entities/
   620→      subscription.entity.ts
   621→      payment-event.entity.ts
   622→    dto/
   623→      create-checkout.dto.ts
   624→      subscription-response.dto.ts
   625→```
   626→
   627→### New Web App Components
   628→
   629→```
   630→apps/web/src/
   631→  components/
   632→    editors/
   633→      DocumentEditor.tsx      -- Tiptap wrapper
   634→      SpreadsheetEditor.tsx    -- Univer wrapper
   635→      EditorToolbar.tsx        -- Shared toolbar (save, close, dirty indicator)
   636→    signing/
   637→      SignaturePanel.tsx       -- Sign document UI
   638→      VerifySignature.tsx      -- Verification results
   639→      SignatureStatus.tsx      -- Inline status indicator
   640→    teams/
   641→      TeamSidebar.tsx          -- Team list in sidebar
   642→      TeamSettings.tsx         -- Team management
   643→      InviteMember.tsx         -- Invite flow
   644→    billing/
   645→      PlanSelector.tsx         -- Tier selection
   646→      BillingPortal.tsx        -- Subscription management
   647→
   648→  services/
   649→    editor.service.ts          -- Decrypt-edit-encrypt pipeline
   650→    signing.service.ts         -- ECDSA signing/verification
   651→    teams.service.ts           -- Team key management (client-side crypto)
   652→
   653→  stores/
   654→    editor.store.ts            -- Editor state
   655→    teams.store.ts             -- Team membership and keys
   656→    billing.store.ts           -- Subscription state
   657→
   658→  routes/
   659→    BillingPage.tsx
   660→    TeamSettingsPage.tsx
   661→```
   662→
   663→### Communication Between Components
   664→
   665→```
   666→EditorComponent -> editor.service (decrypt/encrypt) -> upload.service (IPFS) -> ipns.service (metadata)
   667→                                                                            |
   668→SigningComponent -> signing.service (ECDSA) -> folder.store (metadata update) -> ipns.service
   669→                                                                            |
   670→TeamsComponent -> teams.service (key mgmt) -> API /teams/* endpoints -> teams module
   671→                                                                            |
   672→BillingComponent -> API /billing/* endpoints -> billing module -> Stripe/NOWPayments
   673→```
   674→
   675→---
   676→
   677→## 8. Data Flow Changes
   678→
   679→### 8.1 Document Edit Flow (New)
   680→
   681→```
   682→User clicks "Edit" on a .cb-doc file
   683→  -> FileListItem routes to DocumentEditor
   684→  -> editor.service.openDocument(fileEntry)
   685→    -> download.service.fetchEncryptedFile(cid)
   686→    -> file-crypto.service.decryptFile(encrypted, fileKey, iv)
   687→    -> JSON.parse(decrypted) -> Tiptap ProseMirror doc
   688→    -> editor.store.setContent(doc)
   689→  -> Tiptap renders document in editor
   690→
   691→User edits...
   692→
   693→User clicks "Save" (or autosave triggers)
   694→  -> editor.getJSON() -> JSON.stringify
   695→  -> file-crypto.service.encryptFile(json, newFileKey, newIv)
   696→  -> upload.service.uploadEncrypted(ciphertext)
   697→  -> ipns.service.updateFileEntry(folder, fileEntry, newCid, newKey, newIv)
   698→  -> vault/unpin old CID
   699→```
   700→
   701→### 8.2 Team Folder Access Flow (New)
   702→
   703→```
   704→User selects team vault in sidebar
   705→  -> teams.store.selectTeam(teamId)
   706→  -> API GET /teams/:id/vault
   707→    -> Returns encrypted team key (ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   708→  -> teams.service.decryptTeamKey(encryptedTeamKey, privateKey)
   709→  -> Decrypt team root folder key with teamKey
   710→  -> folder.store.setRoot(teamRootIpnsName, teamRootFolderKey)
   711→  -> Existing folder navigation works identically from here
   712→```
   713→
   714→### 8.3 Team Member Invitation Flow (New)
   715→
   716→```
   717→Admin clicks "Invite Member" in team settings
   718→  -> Enter invitee's publicKey (or email -> resolve to publicKey)
   719→  -> teams.service.generateInvite(teamKey, inviteePublicKey)
   720→    -> encryptedTeamKey = ECIES(teamKey, inviteePublicKey)
   721→  -> API POST /teams/:id/members { userId, encryptedTeamKey, role }
   722→  -> Server stores team_members row
   723→  -> Invitee can now access team vault on next login
   724→```
   725→
   726→### 8.4 Signing Flow (New)
   727→
   728→```
   729→User opens file and clicks "Sign"
   730→  -> signing.service.signDocument(fileEntry, privateKey)
   731→    -> Download and decrypt file content
   732→    -> contentHash = SHA256(plaintext)
   733→    -> signature = ECDSA_sign(contentHash, privateKey)
   734→    -> Create SignatureRecord
   735→  -> folder.store.addSignature(fileEntry, signatureRecord)
   736→  -> ipns.service.updateFolderMetadata(folder)
   737→```
   738→
   739→---
   740→
   741→## 9. Real-Time Collaboration Assessment
   742→
   743→### 9.1 Verdict: Defer Real-Time Collaboration to M4+
   744→
   745→Real-time collaborative editing with end-to-end encryption is a hard problem. Here is why it should be deferred:
   746→
   747→### 9.2 Technical Challenges
   748→
   749→1. **Encrypted CRDTs:** Standard CRDT implementations (Yjs, Automerge) assume a trusted relay server. For zero-knowledge, updates must be encrypted before transmission. CryptPad solved this with custom encrypted operational transforms, but it took years of development.
   750→
   751→2. **Key distribution for real-time:** Every CRDT update needs to be encrypted. Broadcasting encrypted deltas to N users requires either:
   752→   - Encrypt once with shared key (team key approach -- feasible but requires all participants to have key)
   753→   - Encrypt N times for N participants (O(N) per keystroke -- not scalable)
   754→
   755→3. **Presence and cursors:** Showing other users' cursor positions requires some form of real-time channel. This could be done without compromising zero-knowledge (encrypted WebSocket messages), but adds significant infrastructure.
   756→
   757→4. **Conflict resolution with encryption:** CRDT merge operations need to operate on plaintext. In a zero-knowledge system, the server cannot merge -- all merging must happen client-side, which means every client needs every other client's updates decrypted.
   758→
   759→5. **Infrastructure:** Requires WebSocket server for real-time messaging (not currently in the architecture).
   760→
   761→### 9.3 What M3 Should Build Instead
   762→
   763→**Single-user editing with conflict detection:**
   764→
   765→- User opens document for editing (acquires soft lock)
   766→- If another user opens same document, they see "Currently being edited by [user]"
   767→- Second user can choose to open read-only or force-edit (last-write-wins)
   768→- Lock released on save or close (with timeout fallback)
   769→
   770→This is the same model used by SharePoint's "check-out" feature and is pragmatic for a technology demonstrator.
   771→
   772→### 9.4 Lock Implementation
   773→
   774→```typescript
   775→// Lock stored in team vault metadata (encrypted)
   776→type DocumentLock = {
   777→  lockedBy: string;       // publicKey of lock holder
   778→  lockedAt: number;       // timestamp
   779→  lockTimeout: number;    // auto-release after N seconds (default: 3600)
   780→};
   781→```
   782→
   783→Since locks are in IPNS metadata (encrypted), they are eventually consistent (30s polling). This is acceptable for the advisory lock pattern.
   784→
   785→---
   786→
   787→## 10. Suggested Build Order
   788→
   789→Based on dependency analysis, the recommended phase order for M3 is:
   790→
   791→### Phase 1: Billing Infrastructure
   792→
   793→**Why first:** Billing is independent of other M3 features and the tier system gates access to other features (team member limits, editor limits). Building it first means other features can enforce limits from day one.
   794→
   795→**Scope:**
   796→
   797→- Stripe integration (checkout, portal, webhooks)
   798→- NOWPayments integration (invoice, IPN webhooks)
   799→- Subscription entity and tier enforcement
   800→- Settings page billing UI
   801→
   802→**Dependencies:** None from M3. Uses existing auth and user systems.
   803→
   804→### Phase 2: Team Accounts
   805→
   806→**Why second:** Team infrastructure is needed before team-aware editors and team document signing make sense.
   807→
   808→**Scope:**
   809→
   810→- Team CRUD + member management API
   811→- Team key hierarchy (client-side crypto)
   812→- Team vault initialization
   813→- Team sidebar UI and vault switching
   814→- Permission enforcement
   815→
   816→**Dependencies:** Billing (for team member limits).
   817→
   818→### Phase 3: Document Editors
   819→
   820→**Why third:** Editors are the highest-complexity feature and benefit from having teams in place (team members can test editing flows on shared documents).
   821→
   822→**Scope:**
   823→
   824→- Tiptap document editor integration
   825→- Univer spreadsheet editor integration
   826→- Decrypt-edit-encrypt pipeline
   827→- Autosave with debounce
   828→- Metadata schema extensions (editorType, editorFormat)
   829→- "New Document" / "New Spreadsheet" creation flow
   830→- Advisory locking for team documents
   831→
   832→**Dependencies:** Team accounts (for shared document editing context).
   833→
   834→### Phase 4: Document Signing
   835→
   836→**Why last:** Signing is the simplest M3 feature and is additive to documents that already exist.
   837→
   838→**Scope:**
   839→
   840→- ECDSA signing service (client-side)
   841→- Signature verification
   842→- Multi-signer workflows
   843→- Signature status UI
   844→- Metadata schema extension (signatures array)
   845→
   846→**Dependencies:** Document editors (signing is most useful on editable documents).
   847→
   848→### Build Order Rationale
   849→
   850→```
   851→Billing -> Teams -> Editors -> Signing
   852→  |          |         |          |
   853→  |          |         |          Additive, low dependency
   854→  |          |         |
   855→  |          |         Needs teams for shared editing context
   856→  |          |
   857→  |          Needs billing for tier limits
   858→  |
   859→  Independent foundation
   860→```
   861→
   862→### Estimated Complexity
   863→
   864→| Feature | Backend Complexity | Frontend Complexity | Crypto Complexity | Overall |
   865→|---------|-------------------|--------------------|--------------------|---------|
   866→| Billing | Medium (Stripe/NOWPayments) | Low-Medium | None | Medium |
   867→| Teams | Medium (CRUD + permissions) | Medium | High (key hierarchy) | High |
   868→| Document editors | Low (no backend changes) | High (editor integration) | Low (reuses existing encrypt/decrypt) | High |
   869→| Document signing | Low (metadata only) | Low-Medium | Medium (ECDSA signing) | Medium |
   870→
   871→### Phases Likely Needing Deeper Research
   872→
   873→- **Document editors:** Tiptap and Univer integration specifics, bundle size impact, mobile compatibility
   874→- **Teams:** Key rotation on member removal is complex; needs security review
   875→- **Billing:** NOWPayments recurring API maturity needs validation
   876→
   877→### Phases Unlikely to Need More Research
   878→
   879→- **Document signing:** Uses existing ECDSA primitives, straightforward implementation
   880→- **Billing (Stripe):** Well-documented, mature ecosystem
   881→
   882→---
   883→
   884→## 11. Sources
   885→
   886→### HIGH Confidence (Official Documentation, Authoritative)
   887→
   888→- [Tiptap Editor Documentation](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/getting-started/overview)
   889→- [Tiptap JSON/HTML Export](https://tiptap.dev/docs/guides/output-json-html)
   890→- [Tiptap React Integration](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/getting-started/install/react)
   891→- [ProseMirror](https://prosemirror.net/)
   892→- [Univer Sheets Documentation](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets)
   893→- [Univer React Integration](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/integrations/react)
   894→- [Yjs CRDT Documentation](https://docs.yjs.dev/)
   895→- [Stripe NestJS Integration](https://github.com/reyco1/nestjs-stripe)
   896→- [NOWPayments Recurring Payments API](https://nowpayments.io/blog/recurring-payments-api)
   897→- [NOWPayments Crypto Subscriptions](https://nowpayments.io/crypto-subscriptions)
   898→- [Keeper Encryption Model](https://docs.keeper.io/en/enterprise-guide/keeper-encryption-model)
   899→- [eIDAS Electronic Signature Guide 2026](https://www.portant.co/post/esign-complete-guide-to-electronic-signatures-in-2026)
   900→
   901→### MEDIUM Confidence (Multiple Sources Agreeing)
   902→
   903→- [CryptPad CRDT Blueprints](https://blueprints.cryptpad.org/prototypes/crdt/)
